questions.topic: Two observers counting one flock
questions.learningObjective: interpret the disagreement between two independent counts of one flock
questions.stem: Study group revision: two observers independently counted the same flock of geese, recording 412 and 378 birds. Which statement best describes what their counts show?

options.text: The counts agree exactly, because both observers worked from the same flock.
options.misconception: believes observing the same flock guarantees agreement

options.text: One observer must be wrong, because a flock cannot contain both 412 and 378 birds.
options.misconception: treats any difference as an error by one observer

options.text: The counts prove the flock was moving, because birds were lost between the two counts.
options.misconception: assumes movement is the only source of difference

options.text: The counts differ by 34 birds, about 9 per cent of their average, which is a normal level of counting error.

questions.explanation: The difference is 34 birds and the mean count is 395, giving a relative difference of 8.6 per cent. That size of variation is expected for a moving flock and is not itself an error.
questions.hint: Compare the absolute difference with the mean of the two counts.

options.text: The estimated population is 21.6 birds, because the count must be multiplied by the detection probability.
options.misconception: multiplies by the detection probability instead of dividing

questions.explanation: With a detection probability of 0.6 the count under-represents the true number, so 36 over 0.6 gives 60 birds. A flat function means detectability does not vary with distance, not that all were seen.
questions.hint: Divide the count by the detection probability.

options.misconception: believes equal cluster sizes give no design effect

options.text: The figure shows the four subplots in a cluster are not independent, so the sample has fewer than 32 effective units.
The figure shows the design effect is exactly 4, because each cluster holds four subplots.
options.misconception: equates cluster size with the design effect

options.text: The figure shows the subplots should be analysed separately, since clustering only affects the planning stage.
options.misconception: believes clustering has no effect on the analysis

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A clustered pilot and what it does and does not settle
questions.learningObjective: explain what a clustered pilot can and cannot settle about precision
questions.stem: Study group revision: a pilot survey used 5 clusters of 10 plots and estimated a design effect of 1.25. Explain what this pilot can and cannot settle about the precision of the full survey.

answer.exemplar: The pilot turns 50 nominal plots into an effective sample of 40, so any future sample size calculation should be inflated by 1.25 to achieve the precision a simple random sample would give. It cannot settle the variance of the survey estimate itself, the seasonal variation in cluster means, or whether a larger number of clusters is needed, because only five clusters were sampled and those tell us little about the spread of cluster averages.

questions.explanation: A pilot converts nominal plots into effective units, so 50 plots with a design effect of 1.25 behave like 40 independent plots. It cannot fix the final sample size, since few clusters were sampled.
questions.hint: Divide the nominal plots by the design effect.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A nearest-neighbour index on a one square kilometre plot
questions.learningObjective: design a mapping scheme for measuring the spatial pattern of a planting
questions.stem: Study group revision: the group must decide whether a tree planting is clustered or random. Describe a design that would measure the spatial pattern of the planted trees properly.

answer.exemplar: Map every tree with coordinates across the whole plot, then compute the distance from each tree to its nearest neighbour and take the mean, and compare that with the mean expected for a random pattern of the same density. Do this in a defined area with a buffer so edge trees do not distort the estimate, and report the index alongside the tree density, because the ratio is only meaningful when the density used is correct.

questions.explanation: The index compares mean spacing with the spacing expected for a random pattern at the same density, so mapping must be complete. Buffering edges stops boundary trees biasing the mean.
questions.hint: Map every tree and buffer the plot boundary.

questions.topic: Moran's I on a 4 by 4 grid
questions.learningObjective: identify the extreme value of Moran's I for a checkerboard grid
questions.stem: Study group revision: a 4 by 4 grid of cells is coloured in a perfect checkerboard, alternating 1 and 0. What value does Moran's I take under rook contiguity?

options.text: Zero, because the grid has as many high cells as low cells.
options.misconception: reads a balanced pattern as no spatial association

options.text: Plus one, because neighbouring cells always hold the same value in a checkerboard.
options.misconception: reverses the sign of spatial autocorrelation

options.text: Minus one, because every neighbour pair holds opposite values, the strongest possible negative association.
Plus 0.33, because the checkerboard only partially separates the two classes.
options.misconception: borrows a value from a block pattern instead of a checkerboard

questions.explanation: Moran's I reaches its minimum of minus one when every neighbouring pair differs, which is the checkerboard arrangement. Equal numbers of high and low cells cancel any overall trend.
questions.hint: Think about the strongest possible negative association.

options.misconception: confuses the nugget with the sill and the last lag with the range

options.text: There is no spatial structure, because the semivariance keeps rising instead of flattening.

questions.topic: A dilution series and the reads that would be false negatives
questions.learningObjective: explain what replicate growth patterns say about false negatives and detection limits
questions.stem: Study group revision: a tenfold dilution series is plated in triplicate and growth is seen in every tube down to 10^-4, in one tube at 10^-5 and in none below that. Explain what this pattern says about false negatives and about the limit of detection.

answer.exemplar: The series shows a clean detection limit around 10^-4, because that is the last step at which every replicate grows. At 10^-5 only one of three tubes grew, so the other two are false negatives, meaning viable organisms were present but no growth was recorded. This is why detection limits are quoted from the replicate results rather than from a single dilution, since a step that occasionally grows can easily be mistaken for a genuine detection.

questions.explanation: Growth in every tube at 10^-4 but only one of three at 10^-5 marks the detection limit at 10^-4, and the two silent tubes at 10^-5 are false negatives. The limit is therefore quoted from the replicates.
questions.hint: Compare the replicate counts at each dilution step.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Clusters of four and the design effect
questions.learningObjective: design a clustered survey with an inflated sample size
questions.stem: Study group revision: the group must plan a regional survey of farms where sampling points are grouped by village. Describe a design that produces an honest sample size for the planned survey.

answer.exemplar: Estimate the intraclass correlation from a pilot that samples several villages with several points inside each, then use the design effect of one plus (m - 1) times that correlation, where m is the number of points per village. Inflate the required number of points by that factor to reach the target precision, and if the pilot shows a large effect, add villages rather than points, because more points inside a village buy little extra information once the villages themselves are similar.

questions.explanation: The design effect depends on how similar points within a cluster are, so it must come from pilot data. Adding clusters is the effective response, since points inside a cluster are largely redundant.
questions.hint: Estimate the correlation from a pilot, then inflate the sample size.

options.misconception: believes pilot estimates do not transfer

questions.hint: Divide the number of plots by the design effect.

questions.learningObjective: explain how observer comparison assesses counting error
questions.stem: Study group revision: two observers counted the same flock of gulls independently, recording 430 and 395. Explain how the agreement between observers should be assessed and what a large disagreement would mean.

answer.exemplar: The counts differ by 35 birds, which is 8.5 per cent of their average, and a difference of that size is well within the range of normal observer error on a moving flock. A much larger disagreement would point to a methodological problem rather than noise, such as one observer double counting birds that circled back, or the two working from different points in the flock's movement.

questions.explanation: Two observers on the same flock give a direct check on counting error, and here 35 birds out of 412 is 8.5 per cent. A much larger difference suggests a method problem like double counting.

questions.topic: A strip transect with a flat detection function
questions.learningObjective: design a strip transect survey with a defensible density estimate
questions.stem: Study group revision: the group is designing a strip transect survey of a wetland and must choose its width and repeat visits. Describe a design that produces a defensible density estimate.

answer.exemplar: Choose the strip width from a pilot detection function so that the probability of detection is effectively constant across the transect and falls to nothing at the edges, then repeat the transect several times under similar conditions so that detectability and behaviour are averaged rather than assumed. Record the detection function alongside the counts, since a density estimate is only interpretable alongside the probability of detection on which it rests, and state the closure assumptions used to convert counts into density.

questions.explanation: A density estimate rests on detection being constant, so the width must follow the detection function and be checked by a pilot. Repeat visits under similar conditions average out weather.
questions.hint: Ask what the estimate assumes about detection and timing.

questions.stem: Study group revision: the group is arguing about how to report a detection limit when a dilution series is positive in some tubes and negative in others. Explain how the replicate results should be used and what false negatives mean here.

answer.exemplar: The detection limit should be read from the replicate pattern rather than from the last tube that happened to grow, which in a tenfold series would overstate the sensitivity of the assay. When only one of three tubes grows at the 10^-5 step, the other two are false negatives, meaning viable organisms were present but no growth developed, so the honest limit is the last step at which growth is consistent. Reporting that limit together with the replicate counts lets readers judge the evidence for themselves.

questions.explanation: The detection limit should come from the step where growth is consistently seen, not the last lucky tube. Tubes that should have grown but did not are false negatives, so the assay is missing organisms at low density.
questions.hint: Ask which dilution step growth is consistent across.

answer.exemplar: The pilot shows that the 48 plots carry the information of about 30 independent plots, so any sample size for the regional survey must be inflated by roughly 1.6 to reach the precision a simple random sample would deliver. questions.explanation: A pilot converts 48 nominal plots into about 30 effective plots, the basis for inflating the later sample size. With six clusters it cannot describe how cluster means vary or how the effect changes.

questions.stem: Study group revision: the group is comparing 40 scattered plots with 40 plots arranged in clusters of four. Explain what the design effect means for the precision of each survey and for the size of the difference they can detect.

answer.exemplar: The design effect of one plus (m - 1) times the intraclass correlation, with m the cluster size, measures how much of the apparent sample size is lost to correlation within clusters. With a correlation of 0.05 and clusters of four, the effect is 1.15, so the clustered survey carries the information of about 35 scattered plots. The detectable difference is correspondingly larger, because the standard error rises by the square root of that factor, which is why clustered designs are used for cost reasons rather than precision ones.

questions.explanation: The design effect converts nominal plots into effective ones by measuring within-cluster correlation. The standard error rises by the square root of that factor, so a clustered survey needs more plots for equal power.
questions.hint: Work out one plus (m minus 1) times the correlation.

answer.exemplar: A smooth gradient produces a strongly positive Moran's I because every cell's neighbours hold similar values, and the statistic is then describing a trend in the mean rather than local clustering. answer.exemplar: The design effect, one plus (m - 1) times the intraclass correlation with m the number of sites per catchment, measures how much of the nominal sample size is lost because sites within a catchment share conditions such as geology and land use. questions.learningObjective: judge the significance of a Moran's I value against a reference distribution
questions.stem: Study group revision: the group is asked how confident it should be in a Moran's I value of 0.42 computed on a grid of 25 cells. What should the group check?

options.text: The value is meaningless, because any value above zero must be treated as evidence of clustering.
options.misconception: treats any positive value as significant

options.text: The grid must be square, because Moran's I cannot be computed on a rectangular grid.
options.misconception: believes the grid shape must be square

options.text: The sample size of the study must exceed the number of cells in the grid.
options.misconception: invents a sample size rule for Moran's I

options.text: The value must be judged against a permutation distribution, since 0.42 may well arise by chance.

questions.explanation: Moran's I has an expected value near zero under random arrangement, so 0.42 is only meaningful against the spread produced by rearranging the same values. A permutation test gives that reference.
questions.hint: Compare the value with the spread from rearranging the same data.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A semivariogram read from a table of pairs
questions.learningObjective: identify the range of spatial correlation from a semivariogram
questions.stem: Study group revision: the semivariogram table for soil carbon gives lag distances of 0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125 and 150 metres with semivariances of 0.02, 0.09, 0.18, 0.26, 0.30, 0.30 and 0.30. What is the range of spatial correlation in metres?
questions.explanation: The range is the lag at which the semivariance first reaches the sill of 0.30, which happens at 100 metres. Beyond that the values stay flat, showing no further structure.
questions.hint: Find the distance at which the semivariance reaches its sill.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two observers counting one flock
questions.learningObjective: interpret a pair of independent counts as a reliability check
questions.stem: Study group revision: observer A counted 118 roe deer and observer B counted 132 on the same ground. Which statement about the pair of counts is correct?

options.text: The count must be 125, because the true number lies between the two observers.
options.misconception: averages the two counts as the true number

options.text: The counts differ by 14 animals, about 11 per cent, which is ordinary observer variation.
The counts show that 14 deer were moving between the two sightings.
options.misconception: explains the difference as animal movement

options.text: The counts show the survey is unusable, because observers disagree at all.
options.misconception: treats ordinary disagreement as survey failure

questions.explanation: The difference is 14 animals and the mean count is 125, so the relative difference is 11 per cent. Such differences are normal for moving animals and are why observers count independently.
questions.hint: Express the difference as a fraction of the mean count.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A strip transect with a flat detection function
questions.learningObjective: interpret a map of detections against distance from the transect line
questions.stem: A figure shows a map of a strip transect with the transect line down the middle and circles marking bird positions, densest along the line and thinning towards the edge of the strip. Which reading is correct?

options.text: The birds must be avoiding the transect line, because the circles thin out near it.
options.misconception: misreads the map as showing avoidance of the line

options.text: The birds are evenly spread, because the strip is a fixed width and the pattern looks regular.
options.misconception: assumes a fixed strip gives even distribution

options.text: Detection falls with distance from the line, so the strip width must match the detection function.
The transect must be widened until the circles reach the edge, because the strip is too narrow.
options.misconception: recommends widening rather than modelling detection

questions.explanation: Detections crowding the line and thinning to the edge are the signature of a detection function that falls with distance. The strip width should be set from that function, not simply widened.
questions.hint: Ask whether the pattern is about birds or about detection.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A dilution series and the reads that would be false negatives
questions.learningObjective: design a reporting plan that makes a detection limit credible
questions.stem: Study group revision: the group must convince a reviewer that its detection limit is trustworthy. Describe a design and reporting plan that makes that claim defensible.

answer.exemplar: Present the replicate positives at every dilution, not just the limit, so the reviewer can see where consistency breaks down, and report the limit as the last step with growth in every replicate. Add the inoculum counts used at each step so the concentrations behind the labels can be checked, run uninoculated controls alongside to exclude contamination, and repeat the series on a second occasion so the reader can see the limit is reproducible rather than a one-off result.

questions.explanation: Publishing the replicate positives and inoculum counts lets a reader check the limit, and controls rule out contamination for sporadic growth. Repeating the series shows the figure is reproducible.
questions.hint: Publish every step, not just the limit itself.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Clusters of four and the design effect
questions.learningObjective: justify a survey design choice using the measured design effect
questions.stem: Study group revision: the group must justify its chosen survey design to a reviewer who will ask why the design is not simpler. Describe a design and reporting plan that answers that question.

answer.exemplar: Report the pilot estimates of the intraclass correlation and the resulting design effect, the number of clusters and units per cluster in the final design, and the effective sample size these give against the nominal one, so the cost of the clustered design is stated in the same units as its benefit. If the design effect is close to one, say so and recommend the simpler scattered layout, because then the extra travel buys nothing and the reviewer is right to question it.

questions.explanation: A design effect near one means clustering costs time without buying precision, so the simpler layout should be used. Publishing the pilot estimate and effective sample size lets a reviewer judge the trade-off.
questions.hint: Report the design effect alongside the extra cost of the clustered design.
